<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><span id="id13" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/github-logo.svg" id="g6" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:13/13;" width="13" height="13"></object></span> <a href="https://github.com/McGill-NLP/proxy-metrics" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">McGill-NLP/proxy-metrics</a>
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Progress in language model development is often driven by comparative decisions: which architecture to adopt, which pretraining corpus to use, or which training recipe to apply.
Making these decisions well requires reliable performance forecasts, yet the two commonly used signals are fundamentally limited.
Cross-entropy loss is poorly aligned with downstream capabilities, and direct downstream evaluation is expensive, sparse, and often uninformative at early training stages.
Instead, we propose to construct proxy metrics by aggregating token-level statistics, such as entropy, top-k accuracy, and expert token rank, from a candidate model’s next token distribution over expert-written solutions.
Across three settings, our proxies consistently outperform loss- and compute-based baselines: 1) For cross-family model selection, they rank a heterogeneous population of reasoning models with mean Spearman <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.81</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.81</annotation></semantics></math> (vs. <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.36</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.36</annotation></semantics></math> for cross-entropy loss); 2) For pretraining data selection, they reliably rank 25 candidate corpora for a target model at roughly <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10{,}000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10{,}000\times</annotation></semantics></math> less compute than direct evaluation, pushing the Pareto frontier beyond existing methods; and 3) for training-time forecasting, they extrapolate downstream accuracy across an <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="18\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\times</annotation></semantics></math> compute horizon with roughly half the error of existing alternatives.
Together, these results suggest that expert trajectories are a broadly useful source of signal for assessing model capabilities, enabling reliable performance forecasting throughout the model development life cycle.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language model (LLM) development requires making <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">comparative</em> decisions: which pretraining corpus is better, which post-training recipe increases performance on a target domain, and whether a new model architecture is better than the current frontier.
A common signal for resolving such decisions has been cross-entropy loss, which scales smoothly with compute and extrapolates with remarkable fidelity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
However, the quantity we ultimately care about is downstream performance, not loss. Indeed, models with similar loss can exhibit sharply different downstream capabilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Moreover, LLMs are increasingly judged on hard reasoning tasks where cross-entropy loss over generic text would offer little discriminative signal.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The natural response to resolve this discrepancy has been to fit scaling laws directly for downstream tasks, or to replace accuracy with smoother surrogates such as the likelihood of the correct answer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al., 2025</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhagia et al., 2025</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruan et al., 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brandfonbrener et al., 2025</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
These approaches have been shown to work well when we assume access to plentiful evaluations on a target task, often with a closed answer set, or candidate models that perform above chance.
However, the regimes in which downstream forecasting is most valuable are precisely those in which these assumptions are not met. Evaluations at the frontier of LLMs are often expensive or inaccessible, e.g., requiring human experts, code execution, or an external experimental loop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patwardhan et al., 2026</a>, <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wijk et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Moreover, on hard reasoning tasks, small models or intermediate training checkpoints can all have indistinguishable accuracies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phan et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, which leaves no ordinal signal to fit.
Recent work has also cast doubt on the reliability of downstream scaling laws themselves, finding that many task-level fits break when asked to extrapolate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lourie et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
The obstacle is not only that evaluation is expensive, but also that the quantities we can measure are often too sparse, too late, or too weakly tied to the reasoning process we hope to forecast.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F1.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/cv_combined_scatter.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/432;" width="476" height="432"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S1.F1.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/decision_accuracy.svg" id="S1.F1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/403;" width="476" height="403"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Left.<span id="S1.F1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Ranking models on held-out challenging reasoning tasks (as measured by mean CV Spearman <math id="S1.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>) using our linear RankSVM proxy. Our proxy uses features of the next-token prediction distributions of candidate models over expert reasoning traces. </span>Right:<span id="S1.F1.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Ranking 25 pretraining corpora for a target 1B LLM on the DataDecide testbed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Magnusson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Each method trains small proxy models (4M–90M) on each corpus and attempts to recover the ground-truth corpus ranking defined by the target 1B model’s downstream accuracy. Decision accuracy is the fraction of corpus pairs ranked correctly. Our best proxy metric pushes the Pareto frontier, requiring roughly <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10{,}000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10{,}000\times</annotation></semantics></math> less compute to match the downstream evaluation baseline.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose a different approach for forecasting model performance: <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">compute proxy metrics based on the predictive distribution of the candidate model while it processes an expert solution.</span>
Our intuition is the following.
A final benchmark score records only whether the model succeeded or failed, but an expert trajectory contains a long sequence of local decisions, and a model that cannot yet solve a task may still assign high probability to the crucial steps once they appear in context.
We build on this intuition by passing expert-written trajectories through the candidate in a single forward pass<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          Our approach does not require generating from the candidate model, and hence is extremely efficient.</span></span></span> and computing <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">token-level</em> statistics of its next-token distribution, e.g., entropy, top-<math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy, rank of the expert token, etc.
These statistics are aggregated with weights that emphasize important positions, such as rare tokens or tokens where the candidate is uncertain.
Crucially, because the expert need only provide text, the same construction can use human solutions or traces from closed-weight frontier models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate our approach across three settings that mirror practical decisions in model development (<a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S1.p4.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.55" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.76px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.55 15.55" width="15.55"><g transform="translate(0,15.55) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.78,0) translate(0,7.78)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.08 0 C 7.08 3.91 3.91 7.08 0 7.08 C -3.91 7.08 -7.08 3.91 -7.08 0 C -7.08 -3.91 -3.91 -7.08 0 -7.08 C 3.91 -7.08 7.08 -3.91 7.08 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S1.p4.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> In <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">cross-family model selection</span> (§<a href="#S4" title="4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), where the goal is to rank heterogeneous models on a downstream task without direct evaluation, our best proxy ranks models on held-out reasoning benchmarks in close agreement with their true performance (mean Spearman <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.81</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.81</annotation></semantics></math>, compared with <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.36</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.36</annotation></semantics></math> for cross-entropy loss).
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S1.p4.pic2" class="ltx_picture" height="15.55" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.76px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.55 15.55" width="15.55"><g transform="translate(0,15.55) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.78,0) translate(0,7.78)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.08 0 C 7.08 3.91 3.91 7.08 0 7.08 C -3.91 7.08 -7.08 3.91 -7.08 0 C -7.08 -3.91 -3.91 -7.08 0 -7.08 C 3.91 -7.08 7.08 -3.91 7.08 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S1.p4.pic2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">2</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> In <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">pretraining data selection</span> (§<a href="#S5" title="5 Pretraining Data Selection: Ranking Datasets with Smaller LMs ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), where the goal is to choose among candidate corpora before committing target-scale compute, our proxies reliably rank 25 diverse corpora using only small proxy models, achieving the same ranking quality as direct downstream evaluation at roughly <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10{,}000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10{,}000\times</annotation></semantics></math> less compute.
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S1.p4.pic3" class="ltx_picture" height="15.55" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.76px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.55 15.55" width="15.55"><g transform="translate(0,15.55) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.78,0) translate(0,7.78)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.08 0 C 7.08 3.91 3.91 7.08 0 7.08 C -3.91 7.08 -7.08 3.91 -7.08 0 C -7.08 -3.91 -3.91 -7.08 0 -7.08 C 3.91 -7.08 7.08 -3.91 7.08 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S1.p4.pic3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">3</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> In <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">training-time forecasting</span> (§<a href="#S6" title="6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), we show that proxy metrics follow smooth power laws along training trajectories, enabling extrapolation from early checkpoints, and that downstream accuracy is more predictable as a function of our proxy metric compared to cross-entropy loss or compute, roughly halving extrapolation error across an <math id="S1.p4.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="18\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\times</annotation></semantics></math> compute horizon. The pattern across all settings is the same: generic loss is smooth but task-agnostic, direct evaluation is task-specific but expensive and often uninformative at early training stages, and expert-trajectory proxies provide both smoothness and task-conditioning in a single forward pass.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling laws and downstream forecasting.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Classical scaling laws predict pretraining loss as a function of compute, parameters, and data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
Subsequent work has attempted to extend this predictability to downstream task performance, whether by fitting accuracy directly against compute <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Owen, 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krajewski et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, mapping validation perplexity to downstream error <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, decomposing the prediction into a compute-to-task-loss and task-loss-to-accuracy pipeline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhagia et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, fitting a latent capability axis over benchmark scores from public models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or linking loss thresholds to capability emergence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, these approaches rest on assumptions that are often unmet in practice.
Most require either a family of models trained at multiple scales or non-trivial benchmark scores across a broad population, neither of which is available when evaluating a new architecture or a single training run, or a task whose environment is inaccessible.
Moreover, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lourie et al. (2025)</a></cite> find that only a minority of downstream scaling laws extrapolate reliably, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a></cite> demonstrate that models with nearly identical loss can differ substantially in downstream performance.
A separate line of work predicts smoother task-specific losses across distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brandfonbrener et al., 2025</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mayilvahanan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, avoiding the brittleness of accuracy, but this requires a closed answer set and does not resolve whether task loss tracks the downstream performance we ultimately care about.
In this work, we focus on the problem of relative model ranking and show that proxy metrics derived from a single forward pass over expert trajectories can rank models on held-out tasks and across unseen models.
Moreover, the benchmarks we consider such as graduate-level science <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and olympiad programming <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, are precisely the reasoning tasks on which prior downstream scaling law approaches have not been tested.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Small-scale proxies for pretraining decisions.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A separate line of work asks whether small proxy models can rank candidate pretraining corpora before committing target-scale compute.
Prior approaches have selected domain weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2023</a>)</cite> or data mixtures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> using cheap small-scale runs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Magnusson et al. (2025)</a></cite> systematize this question with DataDecide, a controlled testbed of twenty-five pretraining corpora at fourteen proxy scales, and show that likelihood-style metrics predict the 1B target ranking at <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.01</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01\%</annotation></semantics></math> of target compute.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al. (2026)</a></cite> improve on this with rBridge, which reweights the proxy model’s likelihood by the expert model’s token-level probabilities, defining the previous state-of-the-art Pareto frontier on DataDecide.
Our proxy metrics displace this frontier while requiring only the expert’s tokens, not its probabilities, which opens the door to closed-weight models and human experts as sources of expert signal.
An extended discussion of other related works is provided in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Extended Related Work ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2605.18607v1/method_fig.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/154;" width="476" height="154" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An illustration of our method. We use a candidate model’s next-token prediction distribution at each token of an expert’s trajectory to calculate our proxy metrics.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our goal is to design a proxy signal that is both indicative of a candidate model’s capability on a downstream task, and cheap to evaluate.
We construct this signal from the candidate’s predictive distribution over expert reasoning trajectories for the task instances as illustrated in <a href="#S2.F2" title="In Small-scale proxies for pretraining decisions. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
The intuition is that a model whose distribution often matches the expert’s reasoning at every step is one that has internalized how the task is solved, even when its own generation might have failed.
We assume access to such expert trajectories, whether written by humans or by strong language models.
Reference solutions are already standard for benchmarks of practical interest, and for frontier domains where current LLMs are not yet competent, e.g., drug discovery, protein design, or theorem proving, domain experts working in tandem with AI can provide high-quality reasoning traces.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Preliminaries.</h4>

<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">

<span id="S3.T1.st2.7.8.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.T1.st2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\mathrm{freq}(y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn mathsize="0.800em">1</mn><mo mathsize="0.800em">−</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">freq</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.800em">y</mi><mi mathsize="0.800em">t</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\mathrm{freq}(y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.st2.7.9" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T1.st2.7.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1.7pt;padding-bottom:1.7pt;">
<span id="S3.T1.st2.7.9.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:76.5pt;">
<span id="S3.T1.st2.7.9.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.T1.st2.7.9.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">[0.5pt/2pt]
Gaussian-NLL</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.st2.7.9.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1.7pt;padding-bottom:1.7pt;">
<span id="S3.T1.st2.7.9.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:93.5pt;">
<span id="S3.T1.st2.7.9.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.T1.st2.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="e^{-(\mathcal{L}_{t}-\bar{\mathcal{L}})^{2}/2\sigma_{\mathcal{L}}^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">e</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo mathsize="0.800em">−</mo><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">ℒ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">t</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.800em">−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">ℒ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mn mathsize="0.800em">2</mn></msup><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.800em">2</mn><mi mathsize="0.800em">σ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">ℒ</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mn mathsize="0.800em">2</mn></msup></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-(\mathcal{L}_{t}-\bar{\mathcal{L}})^{2}/2\sigma_{\mathcal{L}}^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a downstream task <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math> with instances <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> and
expert trajectories <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, we pass each
<math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)})</annotation></semantics></math> pair through the candidate model <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>. At each token position <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> we obtain the predictive
distribution <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p_{\mathcal{M}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)}_{&lt;t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathcal{M}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)}_{&lt;t})</annotation></semantics></math>, from which
we calculate a set of <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">core metrics</em> <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">weighting schemes</em> <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The 10 core metrics (<a href="#S3.T1.st1" title="In Table 1 ‣ Preliminaries. ‣ 3 Method ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(a)</span></a>) span three aspects of model–expert
alignment: how often the model agrees with the expert, how concentrated its
distribution is, and how confidently it errs when it disagrees.
Because not every token position is equally diagnostic, we aggregate each core
metric as a weighted average under eight weighting schemes (<a href="#S3.T1.st2" title="In Table 1 ‣ Preliminaries. ‣ 3 Method ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(b)</span></a>)
that emphasize different notions of token importance such as model uncertainty,
disagreement with the expert, or token rarity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Proxy metrics.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each (metric, weighting) pair defines one <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">proxy metric</em>, indexed by <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>.
Given an instance <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)})</annotation></semantics></math> with trajectory of length
<math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>, the proxy metric value is</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{j}(\mathcal{M};\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)})=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T^{(i)}}s_{j}\cdot m_{j,t}^{(i)}\cdot w_{j,t}^{(i)}}{\sum_{t=1}^{T^{(i)}}w_{j,t}^{(i)}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msubsup><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{j}(\mathcal{M};\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)})=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T^{(i)}}s_{j}\cdot m_{j,t}^{(i)}\cdot w_{j,t}^{(i)}}{\sum_{t=1}^{T^{(i)}}w_{j,t}^{(i)}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{j,t}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{j,t}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the core metric value and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{j,t}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{j,t}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the weighting scheme value, both determined by <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>, at position <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> of instance <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{j}\in\{+1,-1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{j}\in\{+1,-1\}</annotation></semantics></math> is a sign convention so that higher values indicate a better model (e.g., <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{j}=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{j}=-1</annotation></semantics></math> for cross-entropy loss). The task-level proxy metric is the mean over instances,</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{j}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{T})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Phi_{j}(\mathcal{M};\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{j}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{T})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Phi_{j}(\mathcal{M};\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}^{(i)}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">With 10 core metrics and 8 weightings, we obtain a library of 80 proxy metrics <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{80}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mn>80</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{80}</annotation></semantics></math>, each assigning a scalar score <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{j}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{j}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{T})</annotation></semantics></math> to a candidate model on a task. When needed, we write <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{80}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>80</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{80}</annotation></semantics></math> for the full vector. The entire library is extracted from a single forward pass per instance, making computation extremely cheap while providing 80 complementary views of how closely the candidate’s predictive distribution tracks the expert’s reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Computing proxy metrics in practice.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In all experiments we compute proxy metrics on the last 1,000 tokens of each expert trajectory, which empirically outperforms using the full trace. We do not filter out trajectories that yield incorrect answers, simulating the realistic setting of imperfect experts. When multiple experts are available, the 80 proxy metrics are averaged across experts and across instances, yielding <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{80}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>80</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{80}</annotation></semantics></math> per (model, task) pair.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A recurring decision in LLM development is choosing which of several candidate models will perform best on a downstream task of interest.
The candidates may span different architectures, pretraining corpora, or post-training recipes, and the target evaluation is often inaccessible, requiring expert graders, code execution, or domain-specific infrastructure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patwardhan et al., 2026</a>, <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wijk et al., 2025</a>)</cite> that cannot be assembled at decision time.
In this section we study whether the proxy metrics from §<a href="#S3" title="3 Method ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> can be used to rank a heterogeneous model population on downstream tasks.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate 18 reasoning-capable language models spanning six model families and six post-training recipes, with sizes ranging from 0.6B to 70B parameters (full list in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Model details ‣ Appendix A Details of Experiments ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>), on six challenging reasoning benchmarks: <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AIME</span> 2025 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Math-AI, 2025</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HMMT</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Balunovic et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPQA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">USACO</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MMLU-Pro</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, and <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SuperGPQA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (details provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Details of Benchmarks ‣ Appendix A Details of Experiments ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>). Together these cover competition math, graduate-level science, broad professional knowledge, and competitive code. Expert trajectories are generated by three frontier open-weight reasoning models: Kimi-K2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team and others, 2026</a>)</cite>, MiniMax-M2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">MiniMax, 2026</a>)</cite>, and Qwen3-Next-80B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. We measure ranking quality by Spearman rank correlation (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>) between proxy scores and downstream accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A natural first question is whether any single proxy metric is universally predictive across these tasks. To investigate, we select the best proxy using downstream scores from all six benchmarks and the full model population, an oracle setting that upper-bounds what any selection procedure can achieve (<a href="#A2.T5" title="In B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tables</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in the Appendix). The best proxy metric attains a mean <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.62" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.62</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.62</annotation></semantics></math>, with per-task correlations ranging from <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.43" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.43</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.43</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.81</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.81</annotation></semantics></math>. No single metric dominates universally. A linear combination of just three proxy metrics, however, reaches <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.88</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.88</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating that the signal is present in the library but distributed across complementary metrics. A practitioner, however, will not have scores on the target task. We therefore ask: <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">given downstream accuracy on a subset of tasks and models, can we find a proxy that generalizes to held-out tasks and unseen models?</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation protocol.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a two-level resampling scheme.
At the <em id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">task</em> level, we perform leave-2-tasks-out cross validation over the six benchmarks, producing <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{6}{2}=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{6}{2}=15</annotation></semantics></math> folds.
In each fold the proxy is selected on the four held-in tasks and scored by the mean <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on the two held-out tasks.
At the <em id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">model</em> level, for each fold we further sample <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the models at random for selection and evaluate ranking correlation on the full model set.
We repeat the model sampling with 20 fixed seeds and report mean <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std across seeds.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ranking models.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The 80 proxy metrics from §<a href="#S3" title="3 Method ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reduce ranking to a low-dimensional learning problem: we seek a function <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathbb{R}^{80}\to\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>80</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathbb{R}^{80}\to\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> whose induced ordering over candidate models tracks their downstream ordering. We compare four model classes of increasing capacity: a <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">univariate proxy</span> <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\Phi)=\Phi_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\Phi)=\Phi_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>; a <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">-sparse proxy</span> <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\Phi)=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\alpha_{k}\Phi_{j_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><msub><mi>j</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\Phi)=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\alpha_{k}\Phi_{j_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math>; a <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">linear RankSVM</span> <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\Phi)=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\Phi)=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> trained under a pairwise hinge loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Herbrich et al., 2000</a>)</cite>; and an <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RBF RankSVM</span> <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\Phi)=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}\,k(\Phi,\Phi_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\Phi)=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}\,k(\Phi,\Phi_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> with a Gaussian kernel, trained under the same objective.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Proxy selection.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the univariate proxy, we select the index <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> that maximizes the mean Spearman <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> between <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{j}(\cdot,\mathcal{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{j}(\cdot,\mathcal{T})</annotation></semantics></math> and downstream accuracy, averaged over tasks <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{in}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{in}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For the <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-sparse proxy, we enumerate all <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{80}{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>80</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{80}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> index triplets and sweep a signed log-spaced grid of coefficient ratios in <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-10^{3},10^{3}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-10^{3},10^{3}]</annotation></semantics></math>, selecting the triplet and ratios that maximize the same objective.
For both RankSVM variants, the parameters are fit on <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathcal{M}_{i}\succ\mathcal{M}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≻</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathcal{M}_{i}\succ\mathcal{M}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> preference pairs induced by the downstream scores.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cross-entropy loss on generic text has been widely used as a predictor of downstream capability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brandfonbrener et al., 2025</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mayilvahanan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
We compute CE loss over 10M tokens from randomly sampled FineWeb <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Penedo et al., 2024</a>)</cite> documents.
We also evaluate rBridge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, which computes expert-probability-weighted CE loss over expert reasoning chains, requiring access to the expert model’s logprobs.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Results and Discussion</h3>

<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.T2.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Leave-2-tasks-out cross-validated Spearman rank correlation (<math id="S4.T2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>) between each proxy and downstream benchmark accuracy. The per-task columns report the mean test <math id="S4.T2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> across all folds in which that task was held out, and the <span id="S4.T2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mean <math id="S4.T2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math></span> column averages over all folds. For learned proxies, values are additionally averaged over 20 random model-subsampling seeds and reported as mean <math id="S4.T2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std across seeds. Best per column is shown in <span id="S4.T2.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bold</span>.</span></figcaption>
