<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2 Results and Discussion ‣ 4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports the leave-2-tasks-out Spearman <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> for all four proxy models and the two loss-based baselines, aggregated across 15 folds and 20 model-subsampling seeds.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Loss-based baselines fail to rank models.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CE loss on FineWeb achieves only <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.36</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.36</annotation></semantics></math>, confirming that a scalar summary of fit to generic text carries little information about relative performance on reasoning tasks. rBridge, which reweights the likelihood along a frontier-model reasoning trace and has access to expert logprobs, fares no better at <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.33" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.33</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.33</annotation></semantics></math>. These results are further illustrated in <a href="#A2.F6" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (left) in the Appendix, where we visualize the loss-based baselines against MMLU-Pro accuracy and find no coherent pattern.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Proxy models show high correlation with performance.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The univariate proxy reaches <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.54" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.54</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.54</annotation></semantics></math>, which is higher than the best loss-based baseline.
The <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-sparse proxy pushes this to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.78" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.78</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.78</annotation></semantics></math>, and the full linear RankSVM reaches <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.81</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.81</annotation></semantics></math>, with the RBF variant tied.
<a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (left) plots downstream accuracy against the linear RankSVM proxy score for each of the six benchmarks in a randomly sampled held-out fold.
Across all six tasks the relationship is monotonic.
<a href="#A2.F6" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (right) in the Appendix zooms into MMLU-Pro, showing that this monotonic relationship holds across different base families and post-training recipes. <a href="#A2.F7" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Loss-based baselines fail across model families. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> in the Appendix show that similar trends hold even when we consider 3 held-out tasks and a lesser percentage of models used for selection.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ranking signal concentrates on a few proxy metrics.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F5" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> in the Appendix shows how often each proxy metric is selected across folds and seeds. The distribution concentrates on a handful of cells.
For the univariate proxy, inverse-frequency-weighted top-1 accuracy, a signal indicating model agreement with expert on rare tokens, dominates.
For the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-sparse proxy, entropy-weighted entropy and frequency-weighted top-5 accuracy are most frequently selected, capturing model uncertainty at positions where the candidate is least committed.
These are precisely the “forking tokens” that <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite> identify as driving the majority of RL training signal in reasoning chains.
Note that this analysis characterizes where the ranking signal concentrates rather than explaining why the proxy works, which does not depend on the selected features being interpretable.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Pretraining Data Selection: Ranking Datasets with Smaller LMs</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before committing to a target-scale pretraining run, a team must choose among various candidate pretraining corpora. The target run may cost millions of dollars, so the decision should ideally rest on evidence collected at a fraction of that budget. The standard approach is to train small proxy models on each candidate corpus and rank them by downstream benchmark accuracy or cross-entropy loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Magnusson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. But at small scale, benchmark accuracy is noisy or at chance, and cross-entropy loss on generic text correlates poorly with downstream performance.
In this section, we ask: <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">can our proxy metrics, computed over small proxy models, rank pretraining corpora without ever evaluating on downstream tasks?</em></p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the DataDecide testbed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Magnusson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which consists of twenty-five candidate pretraining corpora, each used to train proxy models at scales ranging from 4M to 90M parameters, together with realized 1B-parameter target models trained on the same corpora.
The ground-truth ranking of the twenty-five corpora is defined by the mean downstream accuracy of the corresponding 1B target models on the <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OLMES</span> suite of ten multiple-choice benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation metric.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Magnusson et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we measure ranking quality by <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">decision accuracy</em>, which is the fraction of corpus pairs in which the proxy model agrees with the target-scale ranking.
It can be formalized as follows.
Let <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}</annotation></semantics></math> be the set of all pretraining corpus pairs <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(A,B)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(A,B)</annotation></semantics></math> with observed mean OLMES performance for the 1B target LLM as <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{A},y_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{A},y_{B}</annotation></semantics></math> respectively, and the predicted performance by the proxy model is denoted by <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}_{A},\hat{y}_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}_{A},\hat{y}_{B}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively, then decision accuracy is:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S5.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textstyle\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{P}\rvert}\sum_{(A,B)\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{I}\big(\text{sign}(\hat{y}_{A}-\hat{y}_{B})=\text{sign}(y_{A}-y_{B})\big)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi></mrow></msub></mstyle><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>sign</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>sign</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textstyle\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{P}\rvert}\sum_{(A,B)\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{I}\big(\text{sign}(\hat{y}_{A}-\hat{y}_{B})=\text{sign}(y_{A}-y_{B})\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Estimating compute.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure the cost of a ranking method by the fraction of the 1B target’s training FLOPs consumed by the proxy model, following the standard approximation <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{FLOPs}=6ND" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>FLOPs</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{FLOPs}=6ND</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
A method that ranks corpora using only 4M-parameter proxy models operates at roughly <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> of the target compute.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Method.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate each univariate proxy metric on every (corpus, model-size) pair in DataDecide, producing a ranking of the <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math> corpora at each compute budget.
Due to the simpler nature of the OLMES tasks compared to the tasks in §<a href="#S4" title="4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, here we use chain-of-thought (CoTs) produced by Llama-3.3-70B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Llama Team and others, 2024</a>)</cite> as the expert trajectories for computing our proxy metrics.
We compare against two baselines.
The first is the DataDecide downstream task performance baseline, which scores each corpus by the mean OLMES accuracy of the corresponding proxy model.
The second is rBridge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, which reweighs the proxy model’s negative log-likelihood at each token position of the expert’s CoT by the expert model’s token-level probabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Results and Discussion</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (right) plots decision accuracy against compute budget for all methods.
Prior to this work, rBridge defined the state-of-the-art Pareto frontier on DataDecide.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">New state-of-the-art on DataDecide.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our best proxy metric, frequency-weighted top-5 accuracy, pushes this frontier.
At roughly <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> of the target compute, it reaches decision accuracy above <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.85</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.85</annotation></semantics></math>, and at matched compute budgets it dominates rBridge at almost every point where both methods are defined.
To reach comparable decision accuracy using the downstream performance baseline, one must scale proxy models to a budget exceeding <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> of the target, which is roughly <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> times more compute.
This advantage comes under <em id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">strictly weaker assumptions</em>: our proxy metrics require only the expert’s discrete tokens, not its logprobs, enabling closed-weight frontier models as well as human experts to be valid sources.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why proxies are suitable for small models.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We believe that the reason proxy metrics discriminate among corpora at these scales is that a model which cannot solve a problem can still track the CoT written by an expert.
Benchmark accuracy requires the model to produce a correct answer, which may not be possible at such small scales.
But the model’s token-level compatibility with an expert trajectory varies measurably across corpora long before any benchmark score exits the noise floor.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The previous sections showed that proxy metrics can rank models and pretraining corpora for downstream task performance.
But a practitioner often needs to forecast end-of-training capability with a fraction of the training compute expended.
This requires that the proxy evolve predictably with training compute, so that a fit from early checkpoints can be extrapolated to later ones.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training</h3>

<figure id="S6.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S6.F3.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/grid_4.svg" id="S6.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/326;" width="476" height="326"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S6.F3.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/x1.svg" id="S6.F3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/328;" width="476" height="328"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F3.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S6.F3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Extrapolating proxy metrics along the training trajectory.<span id="S6.F3.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <em id="S6.F3.7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Left:</em> pretraining checkpoints of OLMo-3-7B on four reasoning benchmarks. <em id="S6.F3.7.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Right:</em> post-training checkpoints of OLMo-3-7B-Think on four reasoning benchmarks. Filled markers are the training window, stars are held-out checkpoints, solid curves are power-law fits from the training window, and dashed curves are extrapolations. The plots for other benchmarks are provided in <a href="#A2.F10" title="In Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> and <a href="#A2.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> in the Appendix.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">First, we test whether <em id="S6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">we can find proxy metrics that follow a simple functional form along the training trajectory</em>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Experimental setup.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study two trajectories: the pretraining checkpoints of OLMo-3-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olmo et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, evaluated on all six reasoning benchmarks from §<a href="#S4" title="4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and the post-training checkpoints of OLMo-3-7B-Think, evaluated on five (excluding SuperGPQA, on which the model shows negligible improvement).
At each checkpoint we compute univariate proxy metrics and fit a power law <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(t)=a-b\,t^{-c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(t)=a-b\,t^{-c}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We select the proxy via an inner split: fit on the first <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=50\%</annotation></semantics></math> of checkpoints, choose the proxy whose extrapolation to the remainder has the lowest normalized mean absolute error (NMAE), defined as mean absolute error divided by the proxy’s range over training.
The selected proxy is then refit on the full window and evaluated on the held-out checkpoint.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results and discussion.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results are shown in <a href="#S6.F3" title="In 6.1 Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
In pretraining, we fit on checkpoints up to 350K steps and extrapolate to <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\sim}4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}4\times</annotation></semantics></math> the compute.
On all six benchmarks the best selected proxy follows a smooth power law, with mean NMAE of <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.03" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.03</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.03</annotation></semantics></math> across tasks.
In post-training, the proxy extrapolates to nearly <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> the training compute with mean NMAE of <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.038" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.038</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.038</annotation></semantics></math>.
As a sanity check, the best selected proxies also correlate strongly with downstream accuracy at the post-training checkpoints (mean Spearman <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.84" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.84</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.84</annotation></semantics></math> illustrated in Appendix <a href="#A2.F12" title="In Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>), confirming that the extrapolated quantity tracks the ranking we care about.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Downstream Accuracy Is More Predictable from Proxy Metrics</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing approaches for predicting downstream task performance fit exponential functions over validation loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or sigmoids over log-compute <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Owen, 2024</a>)</cite>, but <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lourie et al. (2025)</a></cite> show that the majority of such fits fail to extrapolate reliably.
Hence, we next ask: <em id="S6.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">is downstream accuracy more predictable as a function of our proposed proxy metrics compared to cross-entropy loss or training compute?</em></p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<figure id="S6.F4.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:169.1pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/hellaswag.svg" id="S6.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:224/171;" width="224" height="171"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F4.fig2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S6.F4.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Extrapolating HellaSwag accuracy along the OLMo-3-7B pretraining trajectory. The proxy power-law fit (RMSE <math id="S6.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.003" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.003</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.003</annotation></semantics></math>) tracks the target far more closely than the CE loss exponential (RMSE <math id="S6.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.09" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.09</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.09</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Experimental setup.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use pretraining checkpoints of OLMo-3-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olmo et al., 2026</a>)</cite> across ten OLMES benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
For each benchmark we fit a predictor<math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math>accuracy curve on checkpoints up to <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>80,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> steps and evaluate at the final checkpoint (<math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.4</annotation></semantics></math>M steps, roughly <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="18\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\times</annotation></semantics></math> the fitting horizon).
We compare three predictors: (1) CE loss, via an exponential from FineWeb validation loss to accuracy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al., 2025</a>)</cite>; (2) compute, via a sigmoid against <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log_{10}(\text{steps})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>steps</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_{10}(\text{steps})</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Owen, 2024</a>)</cite>; and (3) proxy metric, via a power law, selected by the inner-split protocol of §<a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results and discussion.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S6.T3" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 6.2 Downstream Accuracy Is More Predictable from Proxy Metrics ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> summarizes the extrapolation RMSE across all ten OLMES benchmarks.
The proxy-based fit achieves a mean RMSE of <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.024" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.024</annotation></semantics></math>, roughly half that of the CE loss predictor (<math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.059" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.059</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.059</annotation></semantics></math>) and the compute-based predictor (<math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.055" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.055</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.055</annotation></semantics></math>).
Even on the tasks where a baseline achieves the lowest RMSE, the proxy-based fit is comparable.
<a href="#S6.F4" title="In 6.2 Downstream Accuracy Is More Predictable from Proxy Metrics ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> illustrates the contrast on HellaSwag: within the training window all fits are strong (<math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}&gt;0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}&gt;0.9</annotation></semantics></math>), but at extrapolation the CE loss fit overshoots (RMSE <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.09" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.09</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.09</annotation></semantics></math>) while the proxy fit tracks the target closely (RMSE <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.003" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.003</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.003</annotation></semantics></math>).
We attribute this to the fact that CE loss and compute are both task-agnostic predictors, whereas the proxy is conditioned on the target task through the expert trajectories, and so its relationship with downstream accuracy is less likely to drift as training progresses.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We proposed proxy metrics computed from token-level statistics of a candidate model’s forward pass over expert reasoning trajectories and showed that they carry substantial information about downstream task capability.
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S7.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.55" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.76px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.55 15.55" width="15.55"><g transform="translate(0,15.55) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.78,0) translate(0,7.78)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.08 0 C 7.08 3.91 3.91 7.08 0 7.08 C -3.91 7.08 -7.08 3.91 -7.08 0 C -7.08 -3.91 -3.91 -7.08 0 -7.08 C 3.91 -7.08 7.08 -3.91 7.08 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S7.p1.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> For <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">cross-family model selection</span> under leave-two-tasks-out cross-validation across 6 reasoning benchmarks and 18 models spanning 6 base families, a linear ranker over these metrics achieves Spearman <math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.81</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.81</annotation></semantics></math>, compared to <math id="S7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.36</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.36</annotation></semantics></math> for cross-entropy loss.
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S7.p1.pic2" class="ltx_picture" height="15.55" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.76px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.55 15.55" width="15.55"><g transform="translate(0,15.55) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.78,0) translate(0,7.78)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.08 0 C 7.08 3.91 3.91 7.08 0 7.08 C -3.91 7.08 -7.08 3.91 -7.08 0 C -7.08 -3.91 -3.91 -7.08 0 -7.08 C 3.91 -7.08 7.08 -3.91 7.08 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S7.p1.pic2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">2</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> For <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">pretraining data selection</span> on the DataDecide testbed, a single univariate proxy ranks 25 pretraining corpora with decision accuracy above <math id="S7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.85</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.85</annotation></semantics></math> at roughly <math id="S7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> of target compute, displacing the prior Pareto frontier while requiring only the expert’s tokens, not its logprobs.
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S7.p1.pic3" class="ltx_picture" height="15.55" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.76px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.55 15.55" width="15.55"><g transform="translate(0,15.55) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.78,0) translate(0,7.78)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.08 0 C 7.08 3.91 3.91 7.08 0 7.08 C -3.91 7.08 -7.08 3.91 -7.08 0 C -7.08 -3.91 -3.91 -7.08 0 -7.08 C 3.91 -7.08 7.08 -3.91 7.08 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.0pt" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S7.p1.pic3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">3</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> For <span id="S7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">training-time forecasting</span> along the pretraining trajectory of OLMo-3-7B, proxy-to-accuracy fits extrapolate downstream performance across an <math id="S7.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="18\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\times</annotation></semantics></math> compute horizon with roughly half the error of loss-based or compute-based alternatives.
Across all three settings, the mechanism is the same: the candidate model’s token-level distribution over an expert trajectory provides a dense, task-conditioned signal that inherits the smoothness of loss while remaining grounded in the reasoning process that the downstream evaluation is designed to measure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Several important questions remain. Our experiments establish that proxy metrics work across model families and training stages, but the boundaries of this finding are not yet fully mapped: whether the same construction generalizes to mixture-of-experts architectures, to task types beyond reasoning such as long-context retrieval and agentic evaluation, and whether the power-law fits that enable extrapolation hold across model scales and not only along a single training trajectory. A related question concerns the expert itself. We have assumed access to high-quality reasoning traces, but in practice expert quality will vary, and understanding how proxy signal degrades with weaker or noisier experts is important for deployment. Finally, we have treated the eighty proxy metrics as a fixed library and selected among them post hoc. Learning the aggregation function end-to-end, or designing metrics that target specific failure modes of downstream evaluation, could close the remaining gap between the oracle upper bound and the cross-validated performance we report.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our experimental scope has boundaries that should inform how the results are interpreted.</p>
</div>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model and checkpoint coverage.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The cross-family experiment evaluates 18 models spanning six base families and six post-training recipes. This covers most of the major open-weight reasoning-capable models available while this work was done, but the population is still modest. The training-time forecasting experiments (§<a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a>, §<a href="#S6.SS2" title="6.2 Downstream Accuracy Is More Predictable from Proxy Metrics ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.2</span></a>) rely entirely on checkpoints from OLMo-3-7B and OLMo-3-7B-Think. We chose OLMo because it publicly releases both pretraining and post-training checkpoints at the granularity needed for power-law fitting. This means the extrapolation results are established on a single architecture and scale, and whether the same power-law regularity holds across model sizes, architectures, or mixture-of-experts models remains an open empirical question.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">No universal proxy metric.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">No single proxy metric dominates across all settings. The best univariate proxy for cross-family ranking is not the same as the best proxy for data selection or for extrapolating any particular benchmark. In practice, the specific proxy metric that works best will depend on the available held-in benchmarks, the model population, and hyperparameters of the selection procedure such as the inner-split fraction and the training-window size used for fitting. We have not conducted a systematic sensitivity analysis over these choices. The oracle gap (<a href="#A2.T5" title="In B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) shows that the 80-dimensional library contains enough signal to reach <math id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.88</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.88</annotation></semantics></math> with just three features, but extracting that signal reliably under realistic selection constraints is challenging.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task coverage.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The cross-family ranking experiment focuses on challenging reasoning benchmarks, while the data selection and downstream extrapolation experiments use OLMES, a suite of non-reasoning multiple-choice tasks. This split is driven by resource constraints: DataDecide provides a controlled testbed only for OLMES, and, to the best of our knowledge, no comparable infrastructure exists for reasoning benchmarks at the time of writing. As a result, we have not demonstrated pretraining data selection for reasoning tasks or downstream extrapolation on hard reasoning benchmarks. More broadly, we have also not tested the method on generative tasks (e.g., open-ended writing, translation), long-context benchmarks, or agentic evaluations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Details of Experiments</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Proxy metric definitions</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Below, we describe the exact formulation of each of our core metrics and weighting schemes.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Core metrics.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At each position <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> we compute the <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) cross-entropy loss</span> <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{t}=-\log p_{\mathcal{M}}(y_{t}\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{t}=-\log p_{\mathcal{M}}(y_{t}\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) top-<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy</span> <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="A_{k,t}=\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathrm{top\text{-}}k(\mathcal{M},t)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>top</mi><mtext>-</mtext><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{k,t}=\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathrm{top\text{-}}k(\mathcal{M},t)]</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\{1,2,3,5\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in\{1,2,3,5\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3) entropy</span> <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="H_{t}=-\sum_{v}p_{\mathcal{M}}(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})\log p_{\mathcal{M}}(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})/\log|\mathcal{V}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>v</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>log</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}=-\sum_{v}p_{\mathcal{M}}(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})\log p_{\mathcal{M}}(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})/\log|\mathcal{V}|</annotation></semantics></math> (vocabulary-normalized), <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(4) rank</span> of <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(5) reciprocal rank</span> <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/\mathrm{rank}(y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>rank</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/\mathrm{rank}(y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(6) margin</span> <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{v}p_{\mathcal{M}}(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})-p_{\mathcal{M}}(y_{t}\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{v}p_{\mathcal{M}}(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})-p_{\mathcal{M}}(y_{t}\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})</annotation></semantics></math>, and <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(7) wrong-confidence mass</span> <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\max_{v}p_{\mathcal{M}}(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})\cdot\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{rank}(y_{t})&gt;1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>rank</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{v}p_{\mathcal{M}}(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{&lt;t})\cdot\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{rank}(y_{t})&gt;1]</annotation></semantics></math> that the model places on the wrong token when it misses. Together these metrics span three regimes of model-expert alignment: how often the model agrees with the expert, how peaked the model is, and how badly the model errs when it errs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Weighting schemes.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Not every token position is equally important, e.g.,
function words and punctuation are predicted well by most models and drown out signal.
We therefore introduce per-token weights <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> and aggregate each metric as a weighted average. The eight schemes we consider are: <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) uniform</span> (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=1</annotation></semantics></math>), <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) probability</span> (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=p_{\mathcal{M}}(y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=p_{\mathcal{M}}(y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>), <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3) expert-disagreement</span> (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=1-p_{\mathcal{M}}(y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=1-p_{\mathcal{M}}(y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>), <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(4) entropy</span> (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is vocabulary-normalized so <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>), <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(5) inverse entropy</span> (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=1-H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=1-H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>), <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(6) frequency</span> (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=\mathrm{freq}(y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>freq</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=\mathrm{freq}(y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{freq}(y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>freq</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{freq}(y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> is the frequency of the token in the entire expert trajectories corpus <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>), <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(7) inverse frequency</span> (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=1-\mathrm{freq}(y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>freq</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=1-\mathrm{freq}(y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>), and <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(8) Gaussian-NLL</span> kernel that isolates positions near the typical loss level (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="w_{t}=\exp(-(\mathcal{L}_{t}-\bar{\mathcal{L}})^{2}/2\sigma_{\mathcal{L}}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>exp</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=\exp(-(\mathcal{L}_{t}-\bar{\mathcal{L}})^{2}/2\sigma_{\mathcal{L}}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathcal{L}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathcal{L}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\mathcal{L}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\mathcal{L}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the mean and standard deviation of <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> along the trajectory).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Model details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate 18 reasoning-capable language models spanning six base families (Qwen3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, Qwen2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, Llama3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Llama Team and others, 2024</a>)</cite>, Ministral <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, OLMo3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olmo et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, SmolLM3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bakouch et al., 2025</a>)</cite>) and six post-training recipes (Qwen3, R1-distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI and others, 2025</a>)</cite>, Nemotron <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, Ministral-Reasoning, OLMo3-Think, and SmolLM), with sizes varying from 0.6B to 70B parameters. <a href="#A1.T4" title="In A.2 Model details ‣ Appendix A Details of Experiments ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> lists these 18 models. We treat Qwen3-A3B as a part of the Qwen3 family. We additionally experimented with Ministral-3-14B-Reasoning, but could not obtain consistent performance evaluations on benchmarks (for instance, on some benchmarks it would perform even worse than the 3B model). We consider this a failure of our implementation or lack of reproducibility and hence do not include those results in our analysis.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A1.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="A1.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Models evaluated in the cross-family rank forecasting experiment.</span></figcaption>
<table id="A1.T4.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A1.T4.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T4.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A1.T4.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Base Family</span></th>
<th id="A1.T4.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A1.T4.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Model</span></th>
<th id="A1.T4.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A1.T4.5.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Post-training</span></th>
<th id="A1.T4.5.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A1.T4.5.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Short Name</span></th></tr>
</thead>
