</figure>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We limit generations for all models to a maximum of 28000 tokens. This is to ensure fair comparison across models since some support shorter context lengths than others. In general, we generate with temperature <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=0.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=0.6</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{top-}p=0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>top-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{top-}p=0.95</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{top-}k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>top-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{top-}k</annotation></semantics></math> disabled. Where needed, we followed model-specific overrides based on developer recommendations, for e.g., Ministral <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≤</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq</annotation></semantics></math> 8B uses <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=0.7</annotation></semantics></math>, along with a special system prompt.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Ministral-3-8B-Reasoning-2512" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Ministral-3-8B-Reasoning-2512</a></span></span></span> All benchmark performance evaluations are averaged over 5 random seeds.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Details of Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our experiments in <a href="#S4" title="4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a>, we use six challenging reasoning benchmarks: <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AIME</span> 2025 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Math-AI, 2025</a>)</cite> consisting of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math> problems, <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HMMT</span> Feb-25, Nov-25, and Feb-26 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Balunovic et al., 2025</a>)</cite> consisting a total of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="93" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>93</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">93</annotation></semantics></math> problems, <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPQA</span> main set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite> consisting a total of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="448" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>448</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">448</annotation></semantics></math> problems, <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">USACO</span> competitive programming <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> consisting of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="307" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>307</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">307</annotation></semantics></math> problems, the computer-science and engineering subsets of <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MMLU-Pro</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> consisting a total of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1379" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1379</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1379</annotation></semantics></math> problems, and the hard non-science/engineering subset of <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SuperGPQA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite> consisting of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="382" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>382</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">382</annotation></semantics></math> problems.
Together these cover competition math, graduate-level science, broad professional knowledge, and competitive code.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In our experiments in <a href="#S5" title="5 Pretraining Data Selection: Ranking Datasets with Smaller LMs ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#S6.SS2" title="6.2 Downstream Accuracy Is More Predictable from Proxy Metrics ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.2</span></a>, we use OLMES which consists of MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, HellaSwag <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zellers et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, ARC Challenge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, ARC Easy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, PIQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bisk et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, CommonsenseQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Talmor et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, SocialIQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sap et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, OpenBookQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mihaylov et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, BoolQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, and WinoGrande <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sakaguchi et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Other Experimental Details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments in <a href="#S5" title="5 Pretraining Data Selection: Ranking Datasets with Smaller LMs ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> use DataDecide evaluation results with checkpoints of the default seed. The rBridge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2026</a>)</cite> results are based on our reproduction of their approach as described in their paper. While <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al. (2026)</a></cite> experimented with GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI and others, 2024</a>)</cite> as the teacher, we instead work with an open-weights expert (Llama-3.3-70B) for more reliable access to logprobs. The results for the downstream task performance baseline are taken directly from the DataDecide huggingface repository.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/DataDecide-eval-results" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/DataDecide-eval-results</a></span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments in <a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a> use MiniMax-M2.5 and Qwen3Next-80B as the experts. For pretraining extrapolation, we set the inner-split-fraction as <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>, fit on checkpoints up to step <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="350000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>350000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">350000</annotation></semantics></math> and test the extrapolation at step <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1300000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1300000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1300000</annotation></semantics></math>. To calculate the proxy metrics, since these are pretraining checkpoints, we use a standard chain-of-thought prompt which appends “Let’s think how to answer this question step by step.” to the problem before the expert trajectory. For post-training extrapolation, we fit on checkpoints up to step <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="22000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>22000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">22000</annotation></semantics></math> and test the extrapolation at step <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>40000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40000</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.5 </span>Software and Compute Requirements</h3>

<div id="A1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our code is implemented in PyTorch <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paszke et al., 2019</a>)</cite> and makes use of the HuggingFace Transformers library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wolf et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and the vLLM library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite> for running efficient inference locally on LLMs. All benchmark evaluation and proxy metric calculation experiments were done on our cluster with <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> NVIDIA H100 GPUs with <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>80</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80</annotation></semantics></math> GB memory. Experiments with Kimi-K2.5 were carried out using Together API.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://api.together.xyz/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">https://api.together.xyz/</a></span></span></span>. Obtaining model generations for benchmark evaluations takes around <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> hours on average for a single seed on a benchmark of <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> problems. Computing proxy metrics is extremely fast and takes less than <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> minutes per evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Additional Results and Discussion</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Cross-Family Model Selection</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section provides additional analysis of the cross-family model selection experiment (§<a href="#S4" title="4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). We examine which proxy metrics are selected under cross-validation and oracle access, how the ranking signal compares to loss-based baselines, and how robust the results are to the number of held-out tasks and the fraction of models available for selection.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T5" class="ltx_table">

<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal?</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F5" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> visualizes the frequency with which each of the 80 proxy metrics is selected across all leave-2-tasks-out folds and model-subsampling seeds. In both the univariate and 3-sparse settings, the selection mass concentrates on a small number of cells, with the majority of the 80 proxy metrics never selected.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the univariate proxy (<a href="#A2.F5" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, left), inverse-frequency-weighted top-1 accuracy accounts for <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32\%</annotation></semantics></math> of all selections, more than twice the frequency of any other cell. This metric measures whether the candidate model’s top prediction matches the expert token, but only at positions where the expert token is rare. Frequent tokens, such as punctuation, articles, and common function words, are predicted well by nearly all models and therefore carry little discriminative signal. Upweighting rare tokens isolates the positions where models are most likely to differ: variable names in code, technical terms in science, or key numerical quantities in mathematics. The remaining selection mass spreads across other top-<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy variants (uniform top-1 at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.16</annotation></semantics></math>, uniform top-5 at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.07" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.07</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.07</annotation></semantics></math>) and expert-disagreement-weighted rank (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.12</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.12</annotation></semantics></math>), all of which measure the same broad phenomenon, whether the model agrees with the expert, through slightly different lenses.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A2.F5.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2605.18607v1/cv_metric_weight_heatmap_K1.png" id="A2.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/489;" width="476" height="489" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A2.F5.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2605.18607v1/cv_metric_weight_heatmap_K3.png" id="A2.F5.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/489;" width="476" height="489" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="A2.F5.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Proxy metric selection frequency (normalized) for univariate (<em id="A2.F5.6.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">left</em>) and 3-sparse proxy (<em id="A2.F5.6.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">right</em>). Darker cells are chosen more often. In both cases, a small cluster of proxy metrics accounts for almost all selections. The bulk of the 80 proxy metrics are unused.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A2.F6.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/mmlupro.svg" id="A2.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/440;" width="476" height="440"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A2.F6.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/x2.svg" id="A2.F6.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/407;" width="476" height="407"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F6.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A2.F6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Likelihood-based baselines against a learned proxy.<span id="A2.F6.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <em id="A2.F6.7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Left:</em> the three loss-based baselines (FineWeb cross-entropy loss, uniform expert-trajectory cross-entropy loss, and rBridge) plotted against MMLU-Pro accuracy across 18 language models. Low loss is a weak and non-monotonic indicator of downstream ranking across model families and post-training recipes. <em id="A2.F6.7.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Right:</em> the learned RankSVM (linear) proxy, evaluated on MMLU-Pro in a fold where MMLU-Pro was held out, produces a nearly monotonic relationship with downstream accuracy. The same proxy was not exposed to MMLU-Pro during fitting.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For the 3-sparse proxy (<a href="#A2.F5" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, right), the pattern shifts. The two most frequently selected cells are entropy-weighted entropy (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.16</annotation></semantics></math>) and frequency-weighted top-5 accuracy (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.14" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.14</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.14</annotation></semantics></math>). Entropy-weighted entropy upweights positions where the candidate model is uncertain and asks how diffuse its distribution is at those positions. A model that is uncertain at the right places, the critical reasoning steps, and concentrated elsewhere, is one that has learned the structure of the task without necessarily being able to solve it. Frequency-weighted top-5 accuracy, by contrast, measures agreement with the expert on common tokens. These two signals are complementary: the first captures behavior at hard, high-entropy positions, while the second captures baseline competence on the easy positions. The oracle 3-sparse proxy (<a href="#A2.T6" title="In B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) confirms this complementarity by including both an uncertainty-aware component (expert-disagreement-weighted entropy, coefficient <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+1</annotation></semantics></math>) and a negative coefficient on frequency-weighted top-5 accuracy (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math>), which penalizes models whose agreement with the expert concentrates on frequent tokens where all models perform well.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2605.18607v1/cv_perc_sweep.png" id="A2.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/243;" width="429" height="243" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A2.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of the linear RankSVM proxy as we vary the number of held-out tasks and the fraction of models used for selection. Each cell reports the mean Spearman <math id="A2.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on held-out tasks.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Oracle upper bounds.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.T5" title="In B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> reports the Spearman <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> when the proxy is selected using downstream scores from all six benchmarks and the full model population. Because the proxy is fit and evaluated on the same data, these numbers upper-bound the cross-validated results in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2 Results and Discussion ‣ 4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The univariate oracle reaches <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.62" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.62</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.62</annotation></semantics></math>, with substantial variation across tasks (HMMT at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.43" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.43</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.43</annotation></semantics></math>, SuperGPQA at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.81</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.81</annotation></semantics></math>). The 3-sparse oracle reaches <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.88</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.88</annotation></semantics></math> with per-task correlations between <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.78" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.78</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.78</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.97" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.97</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.97</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating that three complementary proxy metrics contain nearly all the ranking information present in the 80-dimensional library. The gap between the oracle (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.88</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.88</annotation></semantics></math>) and the cross-validated 3-sparse result (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.78" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.78</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.78</annotation></semantics></math>) reflects the difficulty of selecting the right triplet without access to the target task, and suggests that better proxy selection procedures could close part of this gap.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.T6" title="In B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> lists the specific proxy metrics selected under oracle access. The univariate oracle selects inverse-frequency-weighted top-1 accuracy, the same metric that dominates the cross-validated heatmap, providing evidence that the cross-validated selection procedure converges to a genuinely informative signal rather than overfitting to the held-in tasks. The 3-sparse oracle selects three metrics from three distinct regimes of model–expert alignment: expert-disagreement-weighted entropy (an uncertainty signal at positions where the model disagrees with the expert), inverse-entropy-weighted margin (a confidence signal at positions where the model is peaked), and frequency-weighted top-5 accuracy with a negative sign (a correction that discounts agreement on easy tokens). This combination is consistent with the view that ranking heterogeneous models requires measuring not just how often a model agrees with the expert, but how its uncertainty and confidence are distributed across token positions of varying difficulty.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Loss-based baselines fail across model families.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F6" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> contrasts the loss-based baselines with the learned proxy on MMLU-Pro. The left panel plots three loss-based signals, FineWeb cross-entropy (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=-0.52" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.52</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=-0.52</annotation></semantics></math>), uniform expert-trajectory cross-entropy (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=-0.27" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.27</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=-0.27</annotation></semantics></math>), and rBridge (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=-0.33" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.33</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=-0.33</annotation></semantics></math>), against MMLU-Pro accuracy. None of these produces a coherent ranking. Models with very different downstream scores overlap at similar loss values, and the overall relationship is weak and non-monotonic. The right panel shows the linear RankSVM proxy evaluated on a fold where MMLU-Pro was held out. Despite never seeing MMLU-Pro scores during fitting, the proxy produces a nearly monotonic relationship with downstream accuracy (Spearman <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.91" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.91</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.91</annotation></semantics></math>), and this relationship holds across all six base families and seven post-training recipes. The contrast illustrates the central claim of §<a href="#S4" title="4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>: a scalar summary of fit to generic text is a poor predictor of relative downstream performance across a heterogeneous model population, but a small number of task-conditioned token-level statistics can recover the ranking reliably.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2605.18607v1/x3.png" id="A2.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/243;" width="429" height="243" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A2.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of the 3-sparse proxy as we vary the number of held-out tasks and the fraction of models used for selection. Each cell reports the mean Spearman <math id="A2.F8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on held-out tasks.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18607v1/3_sparse_cv_combined_scatter.svg" id="A2.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:286/254;" width="286" height="254"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A2.F9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Ranking LLMs with the <math id="A2.F9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-sparse proxy.<span id="A2.F9.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Downstream accuracy vs. proxy score for each of the six benchmarks on a randomly sampled held-out fold. Same format as <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (left) but using the <math id="A2.F9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-sparse proxy instead of the linear RankSVM.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robustness to held-out tasks and model fraction.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F7" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Loss-based baselines fail across model families. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> show how the linear RankSVM and 3-sparse proxies degrade as we increase the number of held-out tasks (rows) and decrease the fraction of models available for selection (columns). Performance degrades gracefully in both dimensions. For the linear RankSVM, holding out <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=2</annotation></semantics></math> tasks with <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60\%</annotation></semantics></math> of models yields <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.81</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.81</annotation></semantics></math>, and even holding out <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=3</annotation></semantics></math> tasks with <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math> of models still achieves <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.74" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.74</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.74</annotation></semantics></math>. Variance decreases steadily with more models, from <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 0.10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>0.10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 0.10</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 0.01</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math>. The 3-sparse proxy shows a similar pattern. The one regime where performance collapses is <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=5</annotation></semantics></math> held-out tasks (i.e., selecting from a single held-in task), which drops to <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\approx 0.36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.36</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\approx 0.36</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.70" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.70</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.70</annotation></semantics></math> depending on model fraction. This is expected: with only one task for selection, the procedure cannot distinguish proxy metrics that generalize from those that happen to work on that particular task.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Visual comparison of proxy models.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F9" title="In Loss-based baselines fail across model families. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> plots downstream accuracy against the 3-sparse proxy score across all six benchmarks in a randomly sampled held-out fold, providing a counterpart to <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (left). The 3-sparse proxy produces monotonic trends on all six tasks, with somewhat tighter scatter than the linear RankSVM on GPQA and MMLU-Pro but slightly more variance on HMMT. This is consistent with the quantitative comparison in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2 Results and Discussion ‣ 4 Cross-Family Model Selection: Ranking LLMs on Unseen Tasks ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, where the two models achieve similar mean <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.78" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.78</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.78</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.81</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.81</annotation></semantics></math>) but differ on individual tasks.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Training-time Forecasting</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section provides some additional results for the training-time forecasting experiments of §<a href="#S6" title="6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pretraining extrapolation for AIME and SuperGPQA.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F10" title="In Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> extends the pretraining extrapolation of <a href="#S6.F3" title="In 6.1 Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (left) to the two benchmarks not shown in the main figure: AIME and SuperGPQA. On AIME the selected proxy follows a clean power law with NMAE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.007" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.007</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.007</annotation></semantics></math> and train-window <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=0.93" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.93</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=0.93</annotation></semantics></math>, and the extrapolated value lands almost exactly on the held-out checkpoint. SuperGPQA is similarly well-behaved (NMAE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.035" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.035</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.035</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=0.97" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.97</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=0.97</annotation></semantics></math>), with a slightly larger extrapolation gap. Together with the four benchmarks in the main figure (mean NMAE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.034" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.034</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.034</annotation></semantics></math>), these results confirm that the power-law regularity of the proxy is not confined to a subset of tasks: across all six reasoning benchmarks the mean pretraining NMAE is <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.030" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.030</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.030</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Post-training extrapolation for AIME.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F11" title="In Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows the post-training extrapolation on AIME, complementing the set of results in <a href="#S6.F3" title="In 6.1 Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (right). This is the noisiest setting we observe: the training-window points exhibit visible scatter around the fitted power law (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.88</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=0.88</annotation></semantics></math>), and the NMAE is <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.110" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.110</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.110</annotation></semantics></math>, roughly three times larger than the post-training average on the other four benchmarks. We attribute this to the difficulty and noisiness of the task itself. AIME consists of only <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math> problems, all of which are competition-math level difficulty.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Proxy-accuracy correspondence at post-training checkpoints.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The extrapolation experiments predict the <em id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">proxy metric</em> at a future checkpoint. For this prediction to be useful, the proxy must actually track the downstream quantity of interest. <a href="#A2.F12" title="In Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> provides this sanity check by plotting the selected univariate proxy against downstream accuracy across post-training checkpoints of OLMo-3-7B-Think on USACO and HMMT. On USACO the relationship is strongly monotonic (Spearman <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.91" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.91</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.91</annotation></semantics></math>). On HMMT the trend is noisier (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.83" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.83</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.83</annotation></semantics></math>) with wider confidence intervals in general, reflecting the smaller size of the test set and the high difficulty of competition mathematics. Both correlations are well above what would be needed for the extrapolated proxy to serve as a reliable early indicator of downstream ranking, and the mean across all five post-training benchmarks (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.84" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.84</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.84</annotation></semantics></math>, as reported in §<a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Extrapolating Proxy Metric During Training ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a>) confirms that this correspondence holds across the other benchmarks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Proxy metrics selected for per-task downstream accuracy extrapolation.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.T7" title="In Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> expands <a href="#S6.T3" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 6.2 Downstream Accuracy Is More Predictable from Proxy Metrics ‣ 6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> by reporting the identity of the best proxy selected by the inner-split procedure for each of the ten OLMES benchmarks. Two patterns stand out. First, the selected proxies are overwhelmingly top-<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy variants: nine of the ten tasks select a top-<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy metric under some weighting scheme, with <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> ranging from <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math>. The one exception is PIQA, which selects probability-weighted reciprocal rank. This convergence on top-<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> agreement is consistent with the cross-family heatmap in <a href="#A2.F5" title="In Which proxy metrics carry the ranking signal? ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, where top-<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy under various weightings dominates the selected features, and suggests that how often a model places the expert’s token in its top predictions is a broadly informative signal across diverse evaluation settings. Second, the weighting schemes are heterogeneous: inverse-frequency weighting appears on three tasks (Winogrande, CommonsenseQA, SocialIQA), frequency weighting on one (MMLU), entropy weighting on one (BoolQ), and other schemes on the remainder. No single weighting dominates, which is why the full library of eighty proxy metrics is necessary for broad coverage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baseline comparisons for per-task downstream accuracy extrapolation.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F13" title="In Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> shows the direct sigmoid baseline of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Owen (2024)</a></cite> on HellaSwag. Within the training window (up to <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>80</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80</annotation></semantics></math>K steps) the sigmoid fits the data well, but at the held-out checkpoint (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.4</annotation></semantics></math>M steps) it overshoots the true accuracy substantially (RMSE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.11" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.11</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.11</annotation></semantics></math>). <a href="#A2.F14" title="In Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> and <a href="#A2.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Visual comparison of proxy models. ‣ B.1 Cross-Family Model Selection ‣ Appendix B Additional Results and Discussion ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> provide side-by-side comparisons of all three predictors on Winogrande and ARC Challenge. On Winogrande the sigmoid fit undershoots slightly (RMSE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.02</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.02</annotation></semantics></math>), the CE loss exponential overshoots markedly (RMSE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.08" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.08</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.08</annotation></semantics></math>), and the proxy power law tracks the target closely (RMSE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>). ARC Challenge exhibits the same pattern more dramatically: the CE loss exponential diverges (RMSE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.13" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.13</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.13</annotation></semantics></math>), the sigmoid is closer but still off (RMSE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.07" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.07</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.07</annotation></semantics></math>), while the proxy fit remains tight (RMSE <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.02</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.02</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Extended Related Work</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we mention other related works.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Compute-based scaling laws for pretraining loss.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Classical scaling laws connect training compute, parameters, and tokens to a single pretraining cross-entropy loss under controlled architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. These laws are extraordinarily powerful as planning tools when the quantity of interest is loss itself, and the functional form, a power law with additive terms in <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>, is the starting point for virtually every downstream forecasting pipeline that follows, including ours when we extrapolate the proxy metric along a training trajectory in <a href="#S6" title="6 Training-time Forecasting: Proxy Metrics Facilitate Extrapolation ‣ Forecasting Downstream Performance of LLMsWith Proxy Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. They are silent, however, on the quantity practitioners actually care about, which is the score of the trained model on a specific downstream task. Follow-up work extends these laws to over-trained regimes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, data-constrained regimes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Muennighoff et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, inference-aware compute budgets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sardana et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and has sharpened their fitting protocols <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choshen et al., 2025</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Besiroglu et al., 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Porian et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. The proxy metrics we study complement this line by producing a dense, task-specific, and well-behaved scalar that is defined at every training step and obeys its own smooth law, even in regimes where pretraining loss has long since saturated its informativeness about task capability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Forecasting downstream task performance.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A growing line of work converts the pretraining loss into a forecast of downstream accuracy. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al. (2025)</a></cite> propose the exponential map <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=\epsilon-k\cdot\exp(-\gamma x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=\epsilon-k\cdot\exp(-\gamma x)</annotation></semantics></math> from validation perplexity to average downstream top-1 error across many tasks. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhagia et al. (2025)</a></cite> decompose the problem into two stages, <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(N,D)\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(N,D)\to</annotation></semantics></math> task-specific loss on the correct answer <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> ranked-classification accuracy, using compute-efficient ladders at roughly <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\%</annotation></semantics></math> of target compute. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite> extend the two-stage approach to domain-mixed pretraining with FLP and FLP-M. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruan et al. (2024)</a></cite> take a different route with observational scaling laws, fitting a low-dimensional latent capability axis over roughly one hundred public models via PCA on benchmark scores, and showing that agentic and reasoning behaviors become predictable in this latent space. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Owen (2024)</a></cite> fits sigmoidal forms from scaling-estimated loss to BIG-Bench and MMLU across eleven families, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polo et al. (2026)</a></cite> show that benchmark performance is well explained by a handful of latent skills that transfer across families. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krajewski et al. (2026)</a></cite> push the single-recipe direct law further by showing that a two-parameter law on training compute can fit downstream accuracy directly when the task is above chance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The unreliability of downstream scaling laws under realistic constraints.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several recent papers document concrete failure modes of the scaling-law-to-downstream pipeline. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lourie et al. (2025)</a></cite> find that only about <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="39\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>39</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">39\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the tasks studied by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al. (2025)</a></cite> exhibit predictably linear scaling of downstream accuracy with compute, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schaeffer et al. (2025)</a></cite> argue that predicting downstream capabilities of frontier models from scale has remained elusive because argmax-based accuracy degrades the cross-entropy-to-score relationship. Accurate prediction requires modeling probability mass on both correct and incorrect completions. This observation is a direct motivation for the margin and wrong-confidence features in our library, which measure exactly the two sides of this error surface. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Isik et al. (2025)</a></cite> provide a complementary warning. On machine translation, pretraining cross-entropy can continue to fall while BLEU or COMET degrade, so a scalar loss is not even a monotone predictor of the downstream metric. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a></cite> show that models with identical pretraining loss can differ substantially downstream, a direct counterexample to the simplest loss-as-rank hypothesis, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tay et al. (2023)</a></cite> show that the upstream-downstream ordering can invert across architectures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Emergence and the role of continuous metrics.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2022a)</a></cite> coined the term emergent abilities for capabilities that appear absent in smaller models and abruptly present at larger scales, a framing that was interpreted by many as evidence against forecastability. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schaeffer et al. (2023)</a></cite> push back by showing that apparent emergence largely evaporates under continuous and smooth metrics such as log-likelihood, Brier score, or edit distance, with abrupt jumps appearing only when the evaluation collapses the predictive distribution to a discrete score. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2024)</a></cite> strengthen this picture from the opposite direction by arguing that downstream abilities align more cleanly with pretraining loss than with parameter count, and that emergence often reflects a loss threshold. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. (2024)</a></cite> develop PassUntil, a continuous evaluation with effectively infinite resolution that makes per-instance task-solve probability predictable from small-scale models, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Snell et al. (2024)</a></cite> fit emergence laws by finetuning smaller models to shift the emergence point.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Loss-to-loss and cross-distribution prediction.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brandfonbrener et al. (2025)</a></cite> introduce loss-to-loss prediction, fitting shifted power laws that map training loss on one dataset to training or test loss on another and extrapolating up to roughly twenty times the training compute. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mayilvahanan et al. (2025)</a></cite> extend this to thousands of checkpoints, showing that the loss-to-loss trend is robust across architectures and tokenizers. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. (2024)</a></cite> provide cross-family evidence in the same spirit, reporting a Pearson correlation of approximately <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.95</annotation></semantics></math> between bits-per-character and downstream scores across thirty-one LLMs and twelve benchmarks. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Magnusson et al. (2024)</a></cite> propose Paloma as a tokenizer-invariant bits-per-byte benchmark over 546 domains, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2023)</a></cite> show that across the OPT family perplexity predicts in-context learning on seventy-four BIG-Bench tasks better than model size or compute.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Token-level likelihood signals and fine-grained weighting.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several papers have recognized that not every token position carries the same signal. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonen et al. (2023)</a></cite> show that prompt perplexity is a label-free predictor of task performance, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ankner et al. (2025)</a></cite> use small-reference-model perplexity to prune pretraining data and improve downstream accuracy at 3B scale, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thrush et al. (2025)</a></cite> select pretraining documents whose per-document perplexity correlates most strongly with downstream benchmarks. Closest in spirit to our weighting schemes, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al. (2025)</a></cite> introduce LongPPL, which weights perplexity only on key tokens identified by a reference model and achieves a <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.96</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.96</annotation></semantics></math> correlation with long-context benchmarks where uniform perplexity shows almost none. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sorscher et al. (2022)</a></cite> use the teacher’s margin (top minus second-top logit) as a per-example difficulty signal for data pruning, anticipating our use of margin as a token-level feature.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Small-scale proxies for pretraining decisions.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Another line of works asks whether small models can be used to decide between candidate pretraining datasets or recipes before committing target-scale compute. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al. (2024)</a></cite> formalize this as small-scale proxies for large-scale transformer behavior, and <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>P and <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>Transfer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2021</a>)</cite> provide the parameterization that makes such extrapolation work for hyperparameters. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al. (2023)</a></cite> introduce DoReMi, which trains a 280M proxy with Group DRO on excess NLL and transfers domain weights to 8B. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite> introduce RegMix, which fits a regression over 512 1M-parameter proxies to select optimal mixtures at 1B and 7B with roughly <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\%</annotation></semantics></math> of full compute. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Magnusson et al. (2025)</a></cite> construct DataDecide, a large controlled testbed of twenty-five pretraining corpora and fourteen proxy scales, and show that continuous likelihood-style metrics make MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag, MBPP, and HumanEval over <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80\%</annotation></semantics></math> predictable at <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.01</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01\%</annotation></semantics></math> of target compute. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al. (2026)</a></cite> propose rBridge, which aligns the small-proxy NLL with the target task by weighting by a frontier-model reasoning trace.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reasoning traces as supervision and as signal.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reasoning traces have been used most extensively as a training signal. Chain-of-thought prompting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022b</a>)</cite> and self-consistency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> exploit reasoning trajectories at inference, and STaR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and Quiet-STaR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2024</a>)</cite> bootstrap models from generated rationales. Process reward models make the token-level view explicit. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Uesato et al., 2022</a>)</cite> compare process and outcome supervision, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lightman et al. (2024)</a></cite> release PRM800K and show that process supervision dominates outcome supervision, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024a)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2024</a>)</cite> develop automatic step-level process rewards from Monte Carlo rollouts. Two recent methods are particularly close in spirit to ours at the scoring step. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al. (2023)</a></cite> use per-step LM token likelihood together with self-evaluation as an MCTS reward, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cui et al. (2025)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al. (2025)</a></cite> derive implicit token-level process rewards from log-likelihood ratios of outcome-supervised models. All of these works treat trajectories as signals for training or search. Our paper uses trajectories as an evaluation substrate instead.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>
</div>
</div>

  <div class="keyboard-glossary">
    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
